p:1.title: Prop 1
p:1.what: $11.25B in bonds for affordable rental housing, homelessness programs, and veterans' housing.

sides.a: Yes: the state's largest housing commitment in years; Habitat, teachers, and veterans' groups for.
sides.b: No: adds debt service to the general fund; critics say bonds build slowly and expensively.

p:2.title: Prop 2
p:2.what: Doubles the cap on reserve deposits so the state can save more in good years.

sides.a: Yes: bigger reserves so services survive downturns without cuts.
sides.b: No: money parked in reserves is money not spent on current needs.

p:3.title: Prop 3
p:3.what: Keeps the top income tax rates on income over about $371k, which were set to expire, and sends the revenue mostly to K-12.

sides.a: Yes: teachers, nurses, Planned Parenthood; the tax funds schools and has been in place since 2012.
sides.b: No: Chamber and Jarvis argue it pushes high earners out and should sunset as promised.

p:4.title: Prop 4
p:4.what: Lets the state and local governments offer public matching funds to candidates.

sides.a: Yes: less dependence on big donors; cities like LA already do it.
sides.b: No: taxpayer money for politicians' ads; Jarvis against.

p:5.title: Prop 5
p:5.what: A recall election would be a remove-or-not vote only; the successor would be set by law instead of a same-ballot replacement contest.

sides.a: Yes: ends the 2003-style scenario where a replacement wins with a small plurality.
sides.b: No: voters lose the ability to pick the replacement directly.

p:37.title: Prop 37
p:37.what: $25B bond for shared-appreciation loans covering up to 17% of the price of homes under $1.5M, repaid by the buyers.

sides.a: Yes: access to ownership for people who can pay a mortgage but not a down payment; Treasurer Ma for.
sides.b: No: can leave buyers over-leveraged and lifts prices; DSA took no position, preferring the state build rentals.

p:38.title: Prop 38
p:38.what: $8.4B in bonds for immunology research, with a large share directed to a single nonprofit institute.

sides.a: Yes: a research investment on the model of the stem-cell bond.
sides.b: No: half the money goes to one nonprofit tied to the billionaire sponsor; unusual structure.

p:39.title: Prop 39
p:39.short: Voter ID and proof of citizenship
p:39.what: Requires photo ID to vote and documentary proof of citizenship to register.

sides.a: Yes: supporters say it builds confidence in elections.
sides.b: No: suppresses low-income, elderly, and immigrant voters; ACLU and League of Women Voters against.

p:40.title: Prop 40
p:40.what: One-time 5% tax on net worth over $1B, revenue to healthcare and schools.

sides.a: Yes: Bernie Sanders and SEIU-UHW; fewer than 200 households pay it.
sides.b: No: capital flight and valuation fights; Newsom and the Chamber opposed.

p:41.title: Prop 41
p:41.what: Audit and spending-limit rules written so that if it gets more votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is nullified.

sides.a: Yes: framed as accountability for new taxes.
sides.b: No: exists to cancel Prop 40.

p:42.title: Prop 42
p:42.what: Bans taxes on personal property and wealth, retroactive to January 1; a second counter to Prop 40.

sides.a: Yes: a permanent block on wealth taxes.
sides.b: No: a poison pill that ties the state's hands on future revenue.

p:43.title: Prop 43
p:43.what: Raises the threshold for local citizen-initiated special taxes from a majority to two-thirds.

sides.a: Yes: Jarvis says a supermajority protects taxpayers.
sides.b: No: minority rule over local funding; nurses and firefighters against.

p:44.title: Prop 44
p:44.what: Requires community clinics to spend 90% of revenue on direct patient care.

sides.a: Yes: SEIU-UHW says it stops clinic chains from hoarding reserves and overpaying executives.
sides.b: No: the Democratic Party and clinic associations say it adds burden during federal cuts and could close clinics.

p:45.title: Prop 45
p:45.what: Lets projects labeled essential skip environmental review.

sides.a: Yes: faster housing and infrastructure; CEQA lawsuits delay projects for years.
sides.b: No: 'essential' is broad, and it removes the public's main tool against bad projects.

m:A.title: Measure A
m:A.what: Creates an ethics commission, an independent auditor, and a budget analyst; supervisor term limits go from 8 to 12 years.

sides.a: Yes: oversight the county has never had.
sides.b: No: longer term limits for the supervisors who wrote it.
